      Funnel chart: token addresses → issuers → control recipesOpen the complete catalogue map

      Every token address we can find on Solana, read left to right: what it tracks, which issuer programme created it, which control recipe that programme runs on it (the token program plus the extensions that are switched on), and which token program holds it. A circle's area is its number of token addresses (with a floor, so a one-token programme is still a dot); a line's thickness is how many tokens take that step. A hollow circle is a programme with no live tokens. Click an issuer circle for its dossier.

      Many token addresses come from a few issuers, one token program and a handful of recipes, so most tokens are technically alike. A recipe lists what the issuer can technically do to a token: pause it, claw it back, limit it to an allowlist or charge a transfer fee. It says nothing about what the holder owns. That is the horizontal axis in the next section.

      Is the token the official record, and how close is it to the share?

      Up the side, how far the token is the official record (Level 4 top → Level 0 bottom): each step adds one thing. The blockchain is the official record of who owns it; then the token moves without anyone’s approval; then holding it is enough to redeem, without the issuer; then a theft or court order can be corrected on the ledger.

      Across, how close you are to owning the share (0 left → 4 right): what the holder legally owns: price exposure only, an unsecured claim on the issuer, a claim secured over collateral, a beneficial interest in shares held for holders, or the registered share itself.

      Each dot is one issuer programme, sized by the log of its total Solana DEX liquidity (floored, so an illiquid programme is still visible). Click a dot for the dossier. The bottom-right corner is a real registered share that barely trades on chain. The middle is a freely transferable wrapper that gives no claim on the share itself. The two scores measure different things and are not added together.

      Programme Traded 24h / tokens Trades 24h Traders 24h Trades / trader Organic Venues Venue spread Last trade Flags

      What this is: trades, traders and organic share are Jupiter's 24-hour aggregates per token address; venues, the last-trade time and the cross-venue price spread come from DexScreener pairs and CoinGecko tickers. Not collected: per-trade on-chain history, counterparty or wallet-level analysis, CEX order-book depth, and exact trade timestamps on DEXs. So a DEX-only token has trades but no last-trade time, and trader counts are per-token sums in which one wallet can appear twice.

      Issuer programmes (…)

      One card per programme. We analyse the programme as a unit: one wrapper, one document set and one set of issuer controls, issued as one or many token addresses. Live programmes come first, ordered by on-chain liquidity. Defunct ones are greyed out and left out of every headline total. Issuer controls are listed as facts and never summed into a score.

      What can you actually do with these tokens today?

      This section counts observed use only. What could work in theory is further down. An asset is counted only when its exact token address appears in a live protocol registry or pool, or an asset-specific live product names it. Generic Token-2022 support and issuer ecosystem logos do not count.

      Where these tokens are usable now

      Each protocol card counts exact Solana token addresses found in the checked live registry, pool or product. Choose an action to answer “where can I do this?” before drilling into an asset.

      The Protocol support column in the token-address table lists the protocols and actions for each asset.       What could work in theory?Open the technical and legal composability analysis

      A token being transferable does not mean a smart-contract lender can safely use it. Each row combines one issuer's legal structure with one on-chain control recipe and asks four different questions: can a protocol hold it, can the lender enforce a borrower default, what can happen after a hack, and what happens when a contract or key becomes inaccessible? Recovery powers cut both ways: they can return stolen tokens to a victim, and they also let the issuer move tokens out of a protocol's custody.

      This table measures what is technically and legally possible. It does not show that any lending protocol lists or accepts the token.

      Every token address

      All exact token addresses found in the universe fetch, loaded from the API 50 at a time, including paused tokens and tokens with no pool. A premium on an illiquid token means little: below roughly $50k of liquidity the on-chain price is a stale AMM print. Reference prices come from three unrelated places and the column names which one. An issuer mark is the sponsor's own number and is not independent.       How to read RWA SonarMethodology, definitions and known gaps

      Where the data comes from

      • Legal facts: hand-researched per issuer from primary documents only (prospectuses, issuer terms and conditions, transfer-agent and regulator records), each with its source URL in the issuer's detail panel. A dossier carries its own confidence rating.
      • The token-address universe: Jupiter token search, read in full on the date shown at the top of this page.
      • On-chain control: the Solana RPC, read directly off each token address's Token-2022 extensions.
      • Reference prices: Pyth where the feed is entitled, an implied price derived from the Ondo registry, or the sponsor's own published mark. The table always names which.

      What a grade means

      Ledger maturity is the site-wide 0–4 level, computed identically to the main assets table: Level 0 unless the chain is the main ledger, then Level 1 unless transfers are unconditional, Level 2 unless redemption is bearer, Level 3 unless a forced-transfer mechanism exists, else Level 4. The score beside it sums ten booleans, +1 for yes and −1 for no.

      Claim depth is a 0–4 level read off the legal form: synthetic exposure, unsecured claim, claim secured over collateral, beneficial interest, registered share.

      Verification strength replaces a yes/no on third-party attestations with a 0–5 scale: none, issuer statement, periodic auditor attestation, daily verification agent, on-chain proof of reserve, transfer-agent register.

      Attestations are positive statements by a named attestor. Findings are negative or neutral facts we observed ourselves, with the evidence attached. No one attests to those.

      Known gaps

      • The universe is a union of searches. No authoritative listing exists. There is no working "all tokenized stocks" call, so the fetch fires many queries by issuer and ticker name. An issuer absent from that query list is invisible here.
      • The forced-transfer pillar grades whether the power exists. It does not grade the process around it. A permanent delegate exists on roughly half the tokens, mostly held by single keys with no published procedure; whether it is bound to a legal process is tracked separately and does not yet move the level.
      • Reference prices are thin. Most tickers have no entitled Pyth feed, so the premium often rests on a quotient derived from an issuer's own registry. That is good enough to spot a 20% gap and too rough to use as a quote.
      • Transfer hooks are reserved but empty. Almost every token reserves the hook slot and none has a hook program installed, so nothing is enforced on chain today. The authority to install one later is kept.
      • Token symbols can differ from tickers. Some issuers truncate their symbols, so joining a token to a real listed ticker needs a lookup table this pipeline does not have. Private companies have no ticker at all.
      • Every field can be absent. A dash means the source does not say, and is never rendered as zero. Missing values are skipped in aggregates.

      Glossary: what the market terms mean here

      Liquidity
      The USD value of the reserves sitting in the token's DEX pools (Jupiter's aggregate over Raydium, Orca and Meteora). It measures depth that can absorb a trade. It does not count trades. A centralised exchange never reports it, so a token that trades mostly on a CEX can show heavy volume and almost no liquidity.
      Volume 24h
      USD traded in the last 24 hours, across all Jupiter routes.
      Organic volume and organic share
      The part of that volume Jupiter classifies as non-bot flow, and organic divided by total. A low organic share means the volume is there but almost none of it looks like real demand.
      Trades 24h
      The number of buys plus sells. Volume is their USD size.
      Traders 24h
      Distinct trading wallets. Summed per token address, so in a programme's row one wallet that traded two of its tokens is counted twice.
      Trades per trader
      Trades divided by traders. A high value points to wash trading: a handful of wallets producing thousands of trades. Above 25 the row is flagged.
      Holders
      Token accounts with a balance, as reported by Jupiter. One person can own many accounts.
      Top-10 %
      The share of supply held in the ten largest accounts.
      Venues
      Distinct DEX ids (from DexScreener pairs) plus exchange markets (from CoinGecko tickers) where the token has a pair.
      Venue spread
      The gap between the lowest and highest price for the same token across venues that traded in the last two hours with real depth (DEX pools ≥ $10k liquidity, exchange markets ≥ $5k 24 h volume); a persistent gap is an arbitrage opportunity, a one-off gap is usually a stale quote.
      Last trade
      The most recent last_traded_at across a token's CoinGecko tickers. It is a per-venue timestamp. Shown as a relative age, with the exact time on hover.
      Not collected
      Per-trade on-chain history; counterparty or wallet-level analysis; order-book depth on centralised exchanges; exact trade timestamps on DEXs. Nothing on this page can tell you who traded, or when a specific on-chain swap happened.
